                                    PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

                                                      §
    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                           §             BEFORE THE
  LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                          §     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
  STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                      §              OF TEXAS

  TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY’S COMMENTS TO PROPOSAL FOR
                PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC § 25.194

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       Texas-New Mexico Power Company (“TNMP”) respectfully submits these comments to
the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) in response to the Commission’s request
for public comment filed on March 16, 2026, related to Rulemaking to Implement Large Load
Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561. TNMP appreciates the opportunity to submit
these comments and looks forward to collaborating with Commission Staff on this project.
                           I.      General comments on Proposed Rule
       TNMP supports the Legislature’s objective to establish standardized interconnection
procedures supporting business development of large load retail customers while minimizing
stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability. TNMP generally agrees that the
proposed rule accomplishes that objective. However, certain portions of the proposed rule must be
modified in order to avoid violating the Commission’s rules and the Public Utility Regulatory Act
(“PURA”). Staff’s proposal for publication imposes significant contractual, financial, and
operational obligations. It is necessary that such obligations align with a framework that preserves
certificated retail service territories, comports with statutory tariff requirements, and ensures just,
reasonable, and non-discriminatory ratemaking.
   A. Definitions of Interconnecting DSP and Interconnecting TSP under Proposed
       §25.194(c)(4)-(5)
       It is imperative that the Commission revise the proposed definitions of “interconnecting
distribution service provider (DSP)” and “Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP).”
The proposed definitions conflict with PURA §37.051(b) and 16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”)
§25.5 regarding which entity has lawful authority to serve retail load, impose service obligations,
and collect customer charges.
       1. Consuming facility location versus point of interconnection location.


                                                  1
         Under PURA §37.051(b), an electric utility may not furnish or make available retail electric
utility service in an area where service is lawfully furnished by another retail electric utility unless
it first obtains a certificate of convenience and necessity (“CCN”) that “includes the area in which
the consuming facility is located.” This statutory requirement is not superseded by PURA
§37.0561. Thus, PURA §37.0561, and the Commission’s new rule implementing it, must be
harmonized with existing law under PURA §37.051(b).
        As proposed, the definition of interconnecting DSP in 16 TAC §25.194 violates PURA
§37.051(b) to the extent it unlawfully defines the DSP based on the “location in which the large
load customer seeks to interconnect.” The location where a large load customer “seeks to
interconnect” may be different than where the large load customer’s “consuming facility is
located.” Those locations may be in different DSPs’ certificated service areas. There is no statutory
basis, or any other legal basis, to require or permit a DSP to provide retail electric delivery service
to a retail customer outside that DSP’s certificated service area.
        To harmonize PURA §§37.0561 and 37.051(b), TNMP proposes the following revision to
the definitions in 16 TAC § 25.194:
        Interconnecting distribution service provider (DSP) -- The electric utility,
        municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is certificated to provide
        retail electric delivery service at the location in which the large load customer’s
        consuming facility is located. seeks to interconnect.

        2. DSPs, not TSPs, must serve retail customers at transmission voltage levels.
        Pursuant to Commission rules, a Distribution Service Provider (DSP) is defined under 16
TAC §25.5(33) as follows:
        Distribution service provider (DSP) -- An electric utility, municipally owned
        utility, or electric cooperative that owns or operates for compensation in this state
        equipment or facilities that are used for the distribution of electricity to retail
        customers, including retail customers served at transmission voltage levels.

        By contrast, a Transmission Service Provider (TSP) is defined under 16 TAC §25.5(142)
as follows:
        Transmission service provider (TSP) -- An electric utility, municipally-owned
        utility, or electric cooperative that owns or operates facilities used for the
        transmission of electricity.

        A large load customer, including large loads served at transmission voltage, receives retail
delivery service and therefore must be served by a DSP, not a TSP, under the Commission’s rules.


                                                   2
 The Commission cannot contravene 16 TAC §25.5 by implementing PURA §37.0561 in a manner
that implicitly converts transmission voltage level retail customers into something other than retail
customers. As set forth above, large load retail customers must be served by the retail electric
utility certificated for the territory in which the customer’s consuming facility is located. Similarly,
pursuant to 16 TAC §25.5(141), a transmission service customer is defined as:
         Transmission service customer -- A transmission service provider, distribution
         service provider, river authority, municipally-owned utility, electric cooperative,
         power generation company, retail electric provider, federal power marketing
         agency, exempt wholesale generator, qualifying facility, power marketer, or other
         person whom the commission has determined to be eligible to be a transmission
         service customer. A retail customer, as defined in this section, may not be a
         transmission service customer.

To harmonize the new rule with PURA and existing Commission rules, the definition of
interconnecting TSP in proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 should be revised as follows:
         Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) -- The electric utility,
         municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that owns and operates the
         facilities necessary for the transmission of electricity to interconnect the large load
         customer to within the ERCOT system.

         3. The proposed definitions contradict Commission rules.
         TNMP’s opposition is not merely conceptual. The proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f) requires
an interconnection agreement to be executed with an interconnecting DSP and, if different than
the interconnecting DSP, an interconnecting TSP. It also requires the interconnection agreement
to specify whether the TSP or DSP “will accept financial security and CIAC from the large load
customer,” and it mandates CIAC for all direct interconnection costs. However, Commission tariff
requirements are explicit under 16 TAC §25.241(b): “No utility shall directly or indirectly collect
any rate or charge… or impose any… practice or regulation different from that which is prescribed
in its effective tariff filed with the commission.” Accordingly, under §25.241(b), CIAC and other
customer charges cannot be lawfully collected by a utility that does not have any tariff applicable
to the large load customer receiving retail service.
         Under 16 TAC §25.5(141), a retail customer may not be, by definition, a transmission
service customer. Additionally, TSP tariffs do not apply to retail customers under §25.192. 1 If a


1
 16 TAC §25.192. Transmission Service Rates. (a) Tariffs. Each transmission service provider (TSP) shall file a tariff
for transmission service to establish its rates and other terms and conditions and shall apply its tariffs and rates on a


                                                           3
 TSP has no tariff governing retail customers, the TSP cannot provide any services to retail
customers, even large load retail customers at transmission voltage.
         No legal basis exists to permit or require new obligations, including financial collections,
for TSPs that cannot lawfully serve the large load and lack an applicable tariff. Accordingly, the
Commission must clarify the §25.194(c)(4) definition of “location” to mean the location of the
consuming facility, consistent with certificated service territory requirements under PURA
§37.051(b) and tariff obligations under 16 TAC §25.241(b).
         Without implementing the necessary changes detailed herein, the Commission risks
adopting a rule that violates tariff and other regulations, and invites disputes and ongoing delays,
contrary to the purpose of §37.0561’s mandate to implement reliable standards.
    B. Interconnection Studies and Allocation of Responsibilities under Proposed §25.194(e)
         Proposed §25.194(e) requires either the interconnecting DSP or TSP to coordinate with
ERCOT to initiate an interconnection study and transmit study-related notifications. In addition to
the statutory and Commission rule conflicts noted above, this proposed subsection would have
unintended practical consequences as well. When paired with §25.194(d)’s requirement that DSPs
and TSPs identify and allocate responsibilities “by agreement,” the rule unnecessarily forces
utilities to renegotiate well established roles and responsibilities and in effect inject additional
costs and delay into a process the Legislature has intended to accelerate.
         PURA § 37.0561(b) requires the Commission to establish standards to interconnect large
load retail and maintain system reliability. Proposing a process that increases negotiation points
and makes study initiation contingent on negotiated responsibilities is the opposite of a reliability-
driven and standardized approach. Under current practice, DSPs coordinate interconnection
studies for retail customers and interface with ERCOT, with TSP participation as needed. The
definition of a DSP in 16 TAC §25.5 expressly includes retail customers served at transmission
voltage level, so the DSP is the proper default coordinator for retail load based study coordination,
with participation by the TSP as needed. Existing roles and responsibilities for overall study
coordination process are neither broken nor inefficient; it merely must be executed on an
accelerated timeline to meet the Legislature’s objectives.




non-discriminatory basis. The tariff shall apply to all distribution service providers (DSPs) and any entity scheduling
the export of power from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region.


                                                          4
         In order to conform with standard DSP retail load coordination duties, TNMP recommends
that the Commission revise §25.194(e) to expressly recognize the DSP as the coordinating entity
for interconnection studies, while preserving appropriate TSP participation, rather than requiring
negotiated reallocations of responsibility that will increase costs and delay interconnections as a
result of negotiations.
    C. Interconnection Agreements and ERCOT Notifications under Proposed §25.194(f)
        Proposed section 25.194(f) requires an interconnection agreement to be executed within 30
days of study completion and authorizes either the DSP or TSP to cancel the request and notify
ERCOT if the deadline is missed. Such an “either party” approach creates an obvious risk of
duplication, inconsistent communication, or inadvertent potential for failure. Experience shows
that established interconnection agreement processes function well when roles are clear and
consistent with existing practice. TNMP recommends that the Commission clarify that existing
interconnection agreement practices remain valid under §25.194(f) and require designation of a
single coordinating entity for ERCOT notifications to avoid duplication or inadvertent
miscommunication.
    D. Intermediate Agreements and Three-Party Agreements under Proposed §25.194(d)
        and §25.194(c)(8)
        1. The three-party agreement requirement is unnecessary.
        Proposed §25.194(d), in conjunction with §25.194(c)(8), requires execution of a three-
party “intermediate agreement” among the large load customer, the interconnecting DSP, and,
where different, the interconnecting TSP, including designation of which entity will accept study
fees and financial security. Even if a TSP could collect fees from a retail customer under a TSP’s
tariff, this requirement represents a significant departure from established statutes (such as PURA
§37.051(b)), tariff regulations (such as 16 TAC §25.241(b)), and existing framework. Ultimately,
introducing unnecessary procedural and jurisdictional complexity into the interconnection process
will inevitably delay interconnections due to extended negotiations among parties with already
distinct and non-overlapping roles.
        The Commission should eliminate the mandatory three-party intermediate agreement
requirement or, at a minimum, strictly limit its purpose to administrative coordination, with no
authority to violate retail service rights, retail obligations, or tariff responsibility by agreement.
        2. Three-party agreements cannot circumvent certificated retail service rights.



                                                   5
         PURA §37.051(b) prohibits a retail electric utility from furnishing or making available
retail electric utility service in another utility’s service area absent a CCN that includes the
consuming facility’s location. Utilities cannot waive, transfer, or reassign certificated service
territory rights or retail service obligations by private agreement. Accordingly, a Commission rule
cannot be implemented in a manner that implies that utilities may reassign statutory retail service
functions outside certificated territories through a “required” intermediate agreement.
        3. TSP tariffs do not govern CIAC and financial security for retail customers.
        The proposed rule also requires the intermediate agreement to identify whether the
interconnecting DSP or TSP will accept “financial security and CIAC” and mandates payment of
a CIAC. Again, under 16 TAC §25.241(b), a utility may not assess charges or impose practices
that are not prescribed in its effective tariff. In addition, under 16 TAC §25.5(141), a retail
customer cannot be a transmission service customer, by definition. A TSP does not, and cannot,
serve retail load, and TSP tariffs do not apply to retail customers under §25.192.
        As a result, a mandatory three-party intermediate agreement cannot lawfully alter which
utility is responsible for serving retail load or impose retail tariff obligations, such as collection of
CIAC, on a utility that lacks certificated authority over the service territory where the large load
retail customer’s consuming facility is located.
        4. Existing bilateral agreements already meet necessary conditions.
        The Commission has long recognized a clear and workable division of responsibilities that
does not require three-party agreements. Under the existing framework, retail utilities and large
load customers address retail service matters through extension agreements or similar retail service
arrangements that comply with CCN requirements. Separately, retail utilities and TSPs address
facilities, construction, and interconnection responsibilities through amended interconnection
agreements, discretionary service agreements, or facilities service agreements. This framework is
well understood, has been deemed legally sufficient, and has enabled timely large load
interconnections without the proposed jurisdictional ambiguity.
        Requiring a three-party intermediate agreement adds negotiation points that do not cure
any deficiency in the current process. Instead, such requirement is likely to increase transaction
costs, complicate accelerated timelines, and heighten the risk of disputes.
        5. The Commission should limit proposed subsection §25.194(d).




                                                   6
         The Commission should continue to allow existing bilateral agreements that comply with
CCN requirements to satisfy §25.194(d) and should eliminate the requirement for a mandatory
three-party intermediate agreement that conflicts with established precedent. Doing so preserves
regulatory clarity, reduces unnecessary administrative and legal steps, and most effectively
advances the Legislature’s objective of facilitating timely large-load interconnections while
maintaining system reliability.
        At a minimum, the Commission must expressly limit §25.194(d) to conform with CCN
and tariff requirements. The rule should clearly state that §25.194 does not authorize any utility to
provide retail electric delivery service outside its certificated territory or to impose or collect retail
tariff charges (including CIAC) from a customer not served under that utility’s
Commission-approved retail tariff.
    E. Power Supply Disclosure under proposed §25.194(d)(7)
        Proposed §25.194(d)(7) requires disclosure of how the large load will procure power and
whether it has onsite generation serving the load. While appropriate, this requirement does not
address future onsite generation plans that may materially affect ERCOT planning and minimum
deliverability assessments. The Commission should expand §25.194(d)(7) to require disclosure of
planned future onsite generation additions, including backup or self-generation resources, over a
defined five-year planning horizon, triggered only upon material change. Such requirement allows
for adequate future planning necessary to ensure overall grid reliability and ongoing ERCOT and
utility power evaluations.
    F. Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee under proposed §25.194(f)(7)
        Proposed §25.194(f)(7) requires a non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW
of contracted peak demand. Subsection (f)(7)(B) further provides that the fee must be paid to the
interconnecting TSP and applied as an offset to that TSP’s rate base. TNMP supports the
Commission in ensuring that large load customers contribute to interconnection costs; in fact, the
current proposal cites to PURA §35.004 as requiring the Commission to ensure large load
customers contribute to recovery of interconnection costs. However, TNMP believes that two
clarifications are necessary to ensure such contributions on a non-discriminatory basis.
        Both PURA §36.003 and 16 TAC §25.234(a) requires rates to be just, reasonable, and not
unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory. As proposed, §25.194(f)(7)(B) directs
the fee to a single TSP and requires a rate base offset applied by that TSP. First, under 16 TAC



                                                    7
 §25.241(b), a utility may not assess charges or impose practices that are not prescribed in its
effective tariff. Standing precedent inherently restricts a TSP’s ability to collect the proposed non-
refundable interconnection fee from a retail customer. Second, it is necessary that the Commission
clarify whether and how the proposed offset, should it be implemented notwithstanding the above
prohibition, benefits the appropriate rate payers who otherwise bear costs otherwise the rule risks
creating a mismatch between who pays and who benefits, ultimately raising nondiscrimination
concerns that utilities are obligated to avoid under PURA §36.003 and 16 TAC §25.234(a).
       Further, the proposal separately requires study fees and CIAC. In order to avoid confusion
and prevent further disputes, the Commission should expressly detail such charge as a “non-
refundable interconnection fee” to be provided to the DSP and clarify how the proposed rate base
offset is intended to apply in light of nondiscrimination obligations and existing recovery practices.
   G. Refund Provisions and Partial Outcomes under proposed §§25.194(g)-(i)
       Proposed §25.194(g)-(i) clearly addresses full withdrawal, non-utilized capacity, and
complete five-year sustainment scenarios but does not clearly address partial withdrawals, partial
energization, or permanent load reductions. Such uncertainty is inconsistent with the statutory
directive to minimize stranded infrastructure costs while maintaining reliability. It is imperative
that the Commission provide insight on refund mechanics regarding partial outcomes.
       In particular, the rule is unclear as to: (1) how refunds are calculated when contracted peak
demand is reduced but not fully eliminated; (2) how financial security is allocated between the
portion of load that is energized and the portion that is not; and (3) how reductions occurring after
initial energization but before the five-year sustainment milestone are to be calculated and
allocated. Without clarification, these provisions create uncertainty for both utilities and customers
and complicate administration of financial security and required refunds under the rules. It is
necessary that the Commission revise §§25.194(g)-(i) to adopt clear, proportional refund
methodologies for partial withdrawals and partial energization.
       TNMP appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and looks forward to
continuing to work with the Commission and Staff on these important issues.




                                                  8
     Respectfully submitted,

       TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY’S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       Texas-New Mexico Power Company (“TNMP”) respectfully submits this executive
summary of its comments to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) in response
to the proposal for publication filed on March 16, 2026, related to the Rulemaking to Implement
Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561.

       1. Precedent retail service obligations cannot be impacted - The proposed rule must
          not modify, reallocate, or expand retail service authority or obligations beyond those
          established under PURA. Section 25.194 must be adopted and applied in a manner
          consistent with PURA §37.051(b), which assigns exclusive retail service obligations to
          the certificated retail electric utility where the “consuming facility is located.” Any
          attempt to redefine service boundaries or allow service outside certificated territories
          would violate statutory requirements and undermine regulatory certainty. TNMP
          recommends explicit language clarifying that retail service rights and obligations
          remain unchanged and are tied to the physical location of the consuming facility.

       2. As proposed, the definition of interconnecting DSP in 16 TAC §25.194 violates PURA
          §37.051(b) to the extent it unlawfully defines the DSP based on the “location in which
          the large load customer seeks to interconnect.” The location where a large load
          customer “seeks to interconnect” may be different than where the large load customer’s
          “consuming facility is located.” Those locations may be in different DSPs’ certificated
          service areas. There is no statutory basis, or any other legal basis, to require or permit
          a DSP to provide retail electric delivery service to a retail customer outside that DSP’s
          certificated service area. Further, under 16 TAC §25.5, a DSP is defined to include
          “retail customers served at transmission voltage levels.” To harmonize PURA and the
          existing rules, TNMP proposes the following revision to 16 TAC § 25.194:
              Interconnecting distribution service provider (DSP) -- The electric
              utility, municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is certificated
              to provide retail electric delivery service at the location in which the large
              load customer’s consuming facility is located. seeks to interconnect.
       3. The Commission’s definition of a Transmission Service Customer under 16 TAC
          §25.5(141) states: “A retail customer, as defined in this section, may not be a
          transmission service customer.” Large load customers, including those served at
          transmission voltage, are retail loads and must be served by the retail electric utility


                                                10
    certificated for the service territory in which the load is physically located. The
   proposed rule cannot permit a TSP to serve retail load, improperly impose retail tariff
   obligations, collect CIAC, or receive retail-related financial security absent a retail
   tariff relationship. Commission rules and PURA make clear that TSPs do not serve
   retail customers and lack applicable tariffs governing retail service to retail customers
   pursuant to 16 TAC §25.241(b). TNMP urges the Commission to revise the proposed
   definitions to align with 16 TAC §25.5:
       Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) -- The electric
       utility, municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that owns and
       operates the facilities necessary for the transmission of electricity to
       interconnect the large load customer to within the ERCOT system.
4. The Commission should expressly recognize the DSP as the coordinating entity for
   large load interconnection studies and ERCOT communications, with TSP
   participation as needed, rather than requiring negotiated reallocations of responsibility
   via contract that will increase costs and delay interconnections.

5. The requirement for mandatory three-party intermediate agreements among the large
   load customer, DSP, and TSP is unnecessary, inconsistent with CCN processes, and
   cannot lawfully alter retail service obligations. Utilities cannot waive, transfer, or
   reassign certificated service territory rights or retail service obligations by private
   agreement. Existing bilateral agreements consistent with CCN requirements should be
   permitted to satisfy §25.194(d), preserving regulatory clarity and reducing
   administrative burden. TNMP recommends eliminating the mandatory three-party
   agreement requirement or strictly limiting its purpose to administrative coordination,
   with explicit safeguards to preserve retail service boundaries and tariff applicability.

6. The Commission should expand power supply disclosure requirements to include
   planned future onsite generation additions over a defined five-year planning horizon,
   to support ERCOT and utility reliability planning.

7. The $50,000 per MW interconnection charge should be expressly identified as a
   non-refundable interconnection fee to the DSP, and the Commission should clarify how
   the rate-base offset mechanism in §25.194(f)(7)(B) provides non-discriminatory
   benefits to all rate payers consistent with cost-causation principles. TNMP
   recommends explicit language detailing the fee’s purpose, application, and rate base
   offset to ensure just, reasonable, and non-discriminatory outcomes.

8. The Commission should revise §§25.194(g)-(i) to adopt clear, proportional refund
   methodologies addressing partial withdrawals, partial energization, and permanent load
   reductions. The current proposal addresses only full withdrawal and complete five year
   sustainment scenarios but leaves ambiguity regarding partial outcomes.

    B. Interconnection Studies and Allocation of Responsibilities under Proposed §25.194(e)
         Proposed §25. 194(e) requires either the interconnecting DSP or TSP to coordinate with
ERCOT to initiate an interconnection study and transmit study-related notifications. In addition to
the statutory and Commission rule conflicts noted above, this proposed subsection would have
unintended practical consequences as well. When paired with §25.194(d)'s requirement that DSPs
and TSPs identify and allocate responsibilities "by agreement," the rule unnecessarily forces
utilities to renegotiate well established roles and responsibilities and in effect inject additional
costs and delay into a process the Legislature has intended to accelerate.
         PURA § 37.0561(b) requires the Commission to establish standards to interconnect large
load retail and maintain system reliability. Proposing a process that increases negotiation points
and makes study initiation contingent on negotiated responsibilities is the opposite of a reliability-
driven and standardized approach. Under current practice, DSPs coordinate interconnection
studies for retail customers and interface with ERCOT, with TSP participation as needed. The
definition of a DSP in 16 TAC §25.5 expressly includes retail customers served at transmission
voltage level, so the DSP is the proper default coordinator for retail load based study coordination,
with participation by the TSP as needed. Existing roles and responsibilities for overall study
coordination process are neither broken nor inefficient; it merely must be executed on an
accelerated timeline to meet the Legislature' s objectives.

    C. Interconnection Agreements and ERCOT Notifications under Proposed §25.194(f)
       Proposed section 25.194(f) requires an interconnection agreement to be executed within 30
days of study completion and authorizes either the DSP or TSP to cancel the request and notify
ERCOT if the deadline is missed. Such an "either party" approach creates an obvious risk of
duplication, inconsistent communication, or inadvertent potential for failure. Experience shows
that established interconnection agreement processes function well when roles are clear and
consistent with existing practice. TNMP recommends that the Commission clarify that existing
interconnection agreement practices remain valid under §25.194(f) and require designation of a
single coordinating entity for ERCOT notifications to avoid duplication or inadvertent
miscommunication.
    D. Intermediate Agreements and Three-Party Agreements under Proposed §25.194(d)
        and §25.194(c)(8)
        1. The three-party agreement requirement is unnecessary.
       Proposed §25.194(d), in conjunction with §25.194(c)(8), requires execution of a three-
party "intermediate agreement" among the large load customer, the interconnecting DSP, and,
where different, the interconnecting TSP, including designation of which entity will accept study
fees and financial security. Even if a TSP could collect fees from a retail customer under a TSP's
tariff, this requirement represents a significant departure from established statutes (such as PURA
§37.051(b)), tariff regulations (such as 16 TAC §25.241(b)), and existing framework. Ultimately,
introducing unnecessary procedural and jurisdictional complexity into the interconnection process
will inevitably delay interconnections due to extended negotiations among parties with already
distinct and non-overlapping roles.
        The Commission should eliminate the mandatory three-party intermediate agreement
requirement or, at a minimum, strictly limit its purpose to administrative coordination, with no
authority to violate retail service rights, retail obligations, or tariff responsibility by agreement.
        2. Three-party agreements cannot circumvent certificated retail service rights.



                                                   5
         PURA §37.051(b) prohibits a retail electric utility from furnishing or making available
retail electric utility service in another utility' s service area absent a CCN that includes the
consuming facility's location. Utilities cannot waive, transfer, or reassign certificated service
territory rights or retail service obligations by private agreement. Accordingly, a Commission rule
cannot be implemented in a manner that implies that utilities may reassign statutory retail service
functions outside certificated territories through a "required" intermediate agreement.
        3. TSP tariffs do not govern CIAC and financial security for retail customers.
        The proposed rule also requires the intermediate agreement to identify whether the
interconnecting DSP or TSP will accept "financial security and CIAC" and mandates payment of
a CIAC. Again, under 16 TAC §25.241(b), a utility may not assess charges or impose practices
that are not prescribed in its effective tariff. In addition, under 16 TAC §25.5(141), a retail
customer cannot be a transmission service customer, by definition. A TSP does not, and cannot,
serve retail load, and TSP tariffs do not apply to retail customers under §25.192.
        As a result, a mandatory three-party intermediate agreement cannot lawfully alter which
utility is responsible for serving retail load or impose retail tariff obligations, such as collection of
CIAC, on a utility that lacks certificated authority over the service territory where the large load
retail customer's consuming facility is located.
        4. Existing bilateral agreements already meet necessary conditions.
        The Commission has long recognized a clear and workable division of responsibilities that
does not require three-party agreements. Under the existing framework, retail utilities and large
load customers address retail service matters through extension agreements or similar retail service
arrangements that comply with CCN requirements. Separately, retail utilities and TSPs address
facilities, construction, and interconnection responsibilities through amended interconnection
agreements, discretionary service agreements, or facilities service agreements. This framework is
well understood, has been deemed legally sufficient, and has enabled timely large load
interconnections without the proposed jurisdictional ambiguity.
        Requiring a three-party intermediate agreement adds negotiation points that do not cure
any deficiency in the current process. Instead, such requirement is likely to increase transaction
costs, complicate accelerated timelines, and heighten the risk of disputes.
        5. The Commission should limit proposed subsection §25.194(d).

         The Commission should continue to allow existing bilateral agreements that comply with
CCN requirements to satisfy §25.194(d) and should eliminate the requirement for a mandatory
three-party intermediate agreement that conflicts with established precedent. Doing so preserves
regulatory clarity, reduces unnecessary administrative and legal steps, and most effectively
advances the Legislature' s objective of facilitating timely large-load interconnections while
maintaining system reliability.
        At a minimum, the Commission must expressly limit §25.194(d) to conform with CCN
and tariff requirements. The rule should clearly state that §25.194 does not authorize any utility to
provide retail electric delivery service outside its certificated territory or to impose or collect retail
tariff charges    (including    CIAC)     from    a       customer   not   served   under   that   utility' s
Commission-approved retail tariff.
    E. Power Supply Disclosure under proposed §25.194(d)(7)
        Proposed §25.194(d)(7) requires disclosure of how the large load will procure power and
whether it has onsite generation serving the load. While appropriate, this requirement does not
address future onsite generation plans that may materially affect ERCOT planning and minimum
deliverability assessments. The Commission should expand §25.194(d)(7) to require disclosure of
planned future onsite generation additions, including backup or self-generation resources, over a
defined five-year planning horizon, triggered only upon material change. Such requirement allows
for adequate future planning necessary to ensure overall grid reliability and ongoing ERCOT and
utility power evaluations.
    F. Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee under proposed §25.194(f)(7)
        Proposed §25.194(f)(7) requires a non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW
of contracted peak demand. Subsection (f)(7)(B) further provides that the fee must be paid to the
interconnecting TSP and applied as an offset to that TSP' s rate base. TNMP supports the
Commission in ensuring that large load customers contribute to interconnection costs; in fact, the
current proposal cites to PURA §35.004 as requiring the Commission to ensure large load
customers contribute to recovery of interconnection costs. However, TNMP believes that two
clarifications are necessary to ensure such contributions on a non-discriminatory basis.
        Both PURA §36.003 and 16 TAC §25.234(a) requires rates to be just, reasonable, and not
unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory. As proposed, §25.194(f)(7)(B) directs
the fee to a single TSP and requires a rate base offset applied by that TSP. First, under 16 TAC



                                                      7
 §25.241(b), a utility may not assess charges or impose practices that are not prescribed in its
effective tariff. Standing precedent inherently restricts a TSP' s ability to collect the proposed non-
refundable interconnection fee from a retail customer. Second, it is necessary that the Commission
clarify whether and how the proposed offset, should it be implemented notwithstanding the above
prohibition, benefits the appropriate rate payers who otherwise bear costs otherwise the rule risks
creating a mismatch between who pays and who benefits, ultimately raising nondiscrimination
concerns that utilities are obligated to avoid under PURA §36.003 and 16 TAC §25.234(a).
       Further, the proposal separately requires study fees and CIAC. In order to avoid confusion
and prevent further disputes, the Commission should expressly detail such charge as a "non-
refundable interconnection fee" to be provided to the DSP and clarify how the proposed rate base
offset is intended to apply in light ofnondiscrimination obligations and existing recovery practices.
   G. Refund Provisions and Partial Outcomes under proposed §§25.194(g)-(i)
       Proposed §25.194(g)-(i) clearly addresses full withdrawal, non-utilized capacity, and
complete five-year sustainment scenarios but does not clearly address partial withdrawals, partial
energization, or permanent load reductions. Such uncertainty is inconsistent with the statutory
directive to minimize stranded infrastructure costs while maintaining reliability. It is imperative
that the Commission provide insight on refund mechanics regarding partial outcomes.
       In particular, the rule is unclear as to: (1) how refunds are calculated when contracted peak
demand is reduced but not fully eliminated; (2) how financial security is allocated between the
portion of load that is energized and the portion that is not; and (3) how reductions occurring after
initial energization but before the five-year sustainment milestone are to be calculated and
allocated. Without clarification, these provisions create uncertainty for both utilities and customers
and complicate administration of financial security and required refunds under the rules. It is
necessary that the Commission revise §§25.194(g)-(i) to adopt clear, proportional refund
methodologies for partial withdrawals and partial energization.
